=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer assessment

The Seller’s package is materially seller-favourable. Most importantly, it combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with limitations applying to **all Claims**. Those provisions could undermine protection for the very risks identified in diligence—even where an indemnity appears to address them.

This assessment is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. References to those documents need verification; the Seller’s descriptions are not proof that an issue is resolved.

## 1. Liability regime: protect meaningful recourse

### General warranties: cap, thresholds and time limits

The proposed general warranty regime is:
- **AUD 4.8 million cap:** 20% of the AUD 24 million price.
- **AUD 25,000 de minimis** for each actionable claim.
- **AUD 250,000 deductible basket:** only the excess is recoverable.
- **18-month notification period.**

These protections compound. Several economically meaningful losses might be excluded individually, while qualifying claims suffer a further AUD 250,000 deduction. Eighteen months may also leave insufficient time to discover issues through post-acquisition reporting.

**Push back:**
- Seek a higher general cap and a longer notification period—an opening position of 24–36 months would give the Buyer more opportunity to identify problems.
- Reduce the thresholds and seek a **tipping basket**, so all qualifying losses become recoverable once the basket is exceeded.
- Aggregate claims arising from related facts or a common cause; avoid artificial splitting below the de minimis.
- Ensure timely notification preserves a claim until resolution, including contingent liabilities. Check for any separate, short deadline to commence proceedings.

These are negotiating positions, not legal requirements. Their adequacy also depends on the Seller’s ability to pay and any agreed security or warranty insurance.

### Fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities need separate treatment

“Administrative simplicity” is not a sound reason to give capacity and title warranties the same protection as ordinary business warranties. If the Seller cannot transfer the promised shares, a maximum recovery of AUD 4.8 million would be fundamentally inadequate.

**Push back:**
- Separate title, capacity and authority warranties from the general regime: seek at least a purchase-price cap, no general thresholds, and materially longer survival, subject to applicable law.
- Require dedicated pre-Completion tax protection, including a tax indemnity, with its own cap and survival period aligned with relevant assessment periods and extensions.
- Keep specific indemnities outside the general cap, basket, de minimis and 18-month limit unless a tailored restriction is expressly agreed.
- Do not accept that tax and IP are “settled” merely because the Seller says so. Their substantive wording and limitations still require review.

### The “all Claims” wording could defeat the negotiated protections

Clauses 9.3, 12.3, 12.8, 13 and 20.5 potentially extend warranty limitations to indemnities, covenant breaches, payment obligations and other causes of action. A specific indemnity is of little value if another clause silently caps it or extinguishes it after 18 months.

**Push back:**
- Use a clear liability matrix stating which limitations apply to each claim category.
- Exclude purchase-price adjustments, repayment/payment obligations and other expressly agreed remedies from general warranty limitations.
- Preserve appropriate termination, equitable and specific-performance remedies.
- Include express protection for fraud and fraudulent concealment, and preserve rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review non-reliance wording carefully for its effect on misrepresentation and statutory claims; do not assume every attempted exclusion is effective under Australian law.

## 2. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge: reject a wholesale transfer of diligence risk

The Seller seeks to disclose everything “contained or referred to” in the data room, accounts, registers and public records. That can extend to obscure references and documents not meaningfully presented to the Buyer.

Clause 8.3 goes further: matters merely **discoverable** by the Buyer or its advisers could defeat a claim. That shifts the risk of an undiscovered problem to the Buyer, regardless of the warranty given.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure**, with enough detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter and its relationship to the warranty.
- Reject blanket data-room and public-record disclosure. If any general disclosure is accepted, tightly define its scope and freeze an accessible, indexed archive.
- Reject constructive or imputed knowledge based on what was discoverable, adviser knowledge or information buried in records.
- Prefer no Buyer-knowledge defence; any compromise should be confined to actual knowledge of specified individuals, without a duty of inquiry.
- Make clear that disclosure or knowledge does **not** qualify specific indemnities, tax protection, completion obligations or agreed price adjustments unless expressly stated.

The Disclosure Letter’s reservations do not cure an underlying defect. Equally, disclosure of an uncertain matter is not proof that a breach or liability exists.

## 3. Bluefen: unresolved consent for a major revenue relationship

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The letter expressly says there is no final written consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

Reasonable endeavours and deemed satisfaction upon delivery of a consent document are inadequate if clause 11.3 imposes substantive conditions.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen consent, together with satisfaction of applicable associated conditions, a genuine Completion condition.
- Require consent covering the actual transaction, without adverse contractual changes, unacceptable costs or termination rights.
- No deemed satisfaction merely because a document is delivered.
- Reserve waiver to the Buyer and provide a long-stop date and exit right if the condition fails.
- Review the underlying clauses and consent itself before concluding the position is resolved.

## 4. Riverlark: debt and security must be dealt with at Completion

Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding, with no final discharge. A release promised after Completion exposes the Buyer to acquiring a company with outstanding debt and encumbered assets.

**Push back:**
- Require an agreed lender payoff statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Arrange repayment and effective security releases at Completion through an agreed funds-flow and release mechanism.
- Verify all relevant guarantees and securities, and require evidence of subsequent register discharges where filing follows Completion.
- Address any change-of-control consent, waiver or default consequences before Completion.

The economics must preserve the **AUD 24 million debt-free/cash-free bargain**. Confirm whether the SPA expresses this through enterprise-value adjustments or another mechanism: Riverlark debt must not become an unadjusted additional Buyer cost, and repayment must not be counted twice.

## 5. Completion bonuses: close the funds-flow gap

The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional, but omitting them from the funds flow does not establish that the Seller will bear them. If the Company pays after acquisition, the Buyer may bear the economic cost.

**Push back:**
- Establish the recipients, conditions, payment dates and applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs.
- Allocate these transaction-related amounts expressly to the Seller.
- Reflect them through payment, a deduction or another appropriate adjustment, with no double counting.
- Obtain protection for later crystallisation of Seller-allocated liabilities.

Do not assume every bonus is already payable: the Completion and continued-employment conditions require review.

## 6. Ironquay: protect ownership and use of the IP, not just the invoice

The record identifies **AUD 180,000 open**, but does not independently establish non-payment. Conversely, there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. If transfer depends on payment of **every SOW3 fee**, covering one invoice may not secure title.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all relevant SOW3 fees and verify cleared payment.
- Obtain any necessary confirmatory assignment and assurance that the Company can continue using the materials.
- Assess the operational importance of the IP; if critical, require resolution before Completion.
- Expand the indemnity beyond the specified payment to losses arising from the identified payment/title defect, including third-party claims and reasonable remediation costs, without general warranty limitations.

Do not treat the open ledger item alone as conclusive evidence that title has failed.

## 7. Export/privacy incident: investigate and allocate the existing risk

The potential export involves approximately **1,240 records**, but access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unresolved. Neither a confirmed reportable breach nor immateriality is established.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a documented investigation into delivery, accessibility, access logs, containment, data scope and applicable legal and contractual obligations.
- Require evidence preservation, prompt updates and appropriate pre-Completion remediation.
- Agree conduct and consultation arrangements without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-Completion incident and resulting investigation, remediation and third-party exposure, with legally recoverable regulatory amounts addressed expressly.

Any retention or additional Completion condition should be proportionate to the investigation results and remaining uncertainty—not an invented loss estimate.

## 8. Supplier renewals: determine their economic substance

Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Neither “ordinary course” nor automatic treatment as debt is established.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together to establish timing, service periods, cancellation rights, accruals and commercial purpose.
- Treat related commitments in aggregate for any interim operating covenant.
- Determine whether each amount is an ordinary post-Completion operating cost, an accrued liability, or an exceptional/Seller-allocated commitment.
- Apply the agreed working-capital, debt and expense definitions consistently, without double counting.

## 9. Other contractual requirements and share title

**Office lease:** The disclosed obligation is notification, not established landlord consent. Verify and require the actual notice obligation to be met; do not invent a consent condition.

**Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not by itself establish a consent requirement for a share sale. Check the complete contract for separate change-of-control provisions.

**Share title:** The share register supports the ownership position but is not complete verification of transferable, unencumbered title. Check the capital structure, constitution, shareholder arrangements, options and other equity rights, transfer restrictions, encumbrances and necessary approvals. Require appropriate title warranties and Completion transfer documents.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Fix the liability architecture:** remove blanket “all Claims” treatment and protect fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and payment obligations separately.
2. **Reject blanket disclosure and deemed knowledge:** diligence access must not substitute for negotiated Seller responsibility.
3. **Make Completion safe:** effective Bluefen consent and associated conditions; Riverlark payoff and release arrangements.
4. **Protect the economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs, debt and any exceptional commitments through consistent price mechanics.
5. **Resolve or specifically allocate identified risks:** Ironquay IP and the export incident.
6. **Verify rather than overstate:** supplier treatment, lease notice, Mossvale restrictions and share title all require underlying-document review.

Finally, assess recoverability: an indemnity from a Seller that distributes the proceeds may offer little practical protection. Consider a proportionate retention, escrow or other credit support for material unresolved exposures.
